items.title: The same element you breathe shields the planet from UV
items.claim: Atmospheric oxygen is O2 — diatomic, vital for respiration. Ozone is O3 — pale blue, pungent, toxic at ground level and protective at altitude. Same element, two molecules, opposite roles.
items.prompt: Why does ozone behave so differently from O2?

options.text: O3's bent three-atom structure with delocalised pi bonding absorbs strongly in the 200-310 nm UV range; O2's MO structure has no comparable visible or near-UV absorption
O3 contains an extra proton per atom

items.reveal:
Ozone is bent with O-O-O angle about 117 degrees and two resonance structures. Its electronic transitions absorb the biologically damaging Hartley UV band.

The Montreal Protocol (1987) phased out CFCs to protect the stratospheric ozone layer. It is the most successful environmental treaty by measurable atmospheric impact. The ozone layer is now slowly recovering.

Ground-level ozone produced by photochemical smog damages lungs at parts-per-billion concentrations. Same molecule, life-saving at 30 km, lung-damaging at the surface.
items.why: Allotropes aren't just minor structural variants — they can be biologically and atmospherically opposite.

items.title: Louis Pasteur separated mirror-image molecules with tweezers
items.claim: In 1848 Louis Pasteur, a 26-year-old chemist, was studying sodium ammonium tartrate crystals from wine. He noticed two distinct mirror-image crystal forms. He separated them by hand with tweezers and showed each rotated polarised light in opposite directions. Chirality was discovered.
items.prompt: What does Pasteur's work imply about biology?

options.text: Living systems prefer one enantiomer over the other — L-amino acids in proteins, D-sugars in DNA. Biological receptors are chiral and distinguish enantiomers like a hand distinguishes left and right gloves

items.reveal_title: A tweezers experiment with deep consequences
items.reveal:
Racemic tartaric acid (a 50:50 mixture of two enantiomers) crystallised in two distinct hemihedral forms. Pasteur, with a hand lens and tweezers, separated the crystals into two piles. Each pile dissolved gave equal and opposite rotations of polarised light. Combined, they cancelled exactly.

The implications were enormous. Carbon atoms with four different groups are chiral; molecules can come in left- and right-handed forms with the same atoms but different spatial arrangements.

Biology is overwhelmingly homochiral. All natural amino acids (except glycine) are L-form; all natural DNA sugars are D-form. Why life chose one hand over the other is still unknown. Some theories invoke parity violation in beta decay, circularly polarised light from neutron stars, or simple chance amplified by autocatalytic prebiotic chemistry.

The thalidomide disaster (1957-1962) drove home that pharmaceutical chirality matters: one enantiomer sedates morning sickness, the other causes severe birth defects.
items.why: A patient observation with hand tools opened a deep window into the molecular geometry of life.
